OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $G$ be a graph with $m$ edges and no isolated vertices. Is the Ramsey number $R(G)$ maximised when $G$ is 'as complete as possible'? That is, if $m=\binom{n}{2}+t$ edges with $0\leq t<n$ then is\[R(G)\leq R(H),\]where $H$ is the graph formed by connecting a new vertex to $t$ of the vertices of $K_n$?
#545: [ErGr75,p.526][Er84b,p.11]
graph theory | 
ramsey theory
A question of Erdős and Graham. The weaker question of whether\[R(G) \leq 2^{O(m^{1/2})}\]is the subject of [546]. (This is true, and was proved by Sudakov [Su11].)
LouisD in the comments has noted this fails for small $m$ (in particular for $2\leq m\leq 5$ and $7\leq m\leq 9$).
This problem is #10 in Ramsey Theory in the graphs problem collection.
Additional thanks to: Sarosh Adenwalla, LouisD, and Desmond Weisenberg

 A 1989 paper of Burr lists the Ramsey numbers for all graphs with $\leq 6$ edges and no isolated points in a very useful table. 
Perusing that table shows that indeed $R(G)\leq 18$ for all such graphs $G$, and so the answer to this question is yes for $m=6$.

 That is in principle true, but for large values, I think it won't make it that much easier.
The Ramsey number for $K_n$ and for the Colex graph $\mathcal C( m)$ where $m=\binom n2+1$ should indeed be the same for large $n$, as in general $R(n,n)>R(n,n-1)+n$ is expected from the exponential behaviour.
Intuitively, once one is forced to have a large red $K_n$, there is somewhere else a vertex with many neighbours in that colour as well.
If one thinks about hard constructions:
for small values, there is a space constraint and the matching $mK_2$ is the one with largest order and thus natural candidate. But this is linear behaviour.
For large values, one could think about "rare" structures like the complement of sparse structured constructions, or multipartite graphs like $K_{t,t}, K_{t,t,t}$.
If the latter would be worse, the exponential behaviour may have a different base.
On the other hand, for the wheel $W_5=K_{2,2,1}$, which has size $8$, $R(W_5)=15<R(K_4) \le R(K_5^{--}).$
Also $26\le R(K_{2,2,2})$ seems to be smaller than $R(K_5)\le 46$.
The potential structured counterexamples I thought about, likely won't beat the clique/ Colex graphs in the limit, but even the explicit comparison may be hard.

 In my previous comment, I indicated that I couldn't find the statement of this problem in [Er84b]. I still don't see the exact statement, but I now see the following sentence (at the top of page 11) "Probably r(G) is maximal if G is as complete as possible." I guess this must be the intended reference. On the other hand, he makes no reference to Graham, so I continued my search.
In https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ExtremeCliques.html, the reference "Some partition theorems in finite graphs" by Erdős and Graham (1973) is given; however, in that paper I was only able to find the statement of the first part (on page 526), not the second part about G having $\binom{n}{2}+t$ edges. 
I noticed that in https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~erdosproblems/erdos/newproblems/ExtremeCliques.html, there is an extra condition which says $n\ge 4$. Presumably, this is because $R(3K_2)=8>6=R(K_3)$
(where $mK_2$ is a matching with $m$ edges).* On the other hand, note that $R(6K_2)=17<18=R(K_4)$. 
Finally I get to my point. I claim that the conjecture is also false for $n=4$ and $t=1$. Let $K_4^{+1}$ be the graph on $5$ vertices and $7$ edges obtained from $K_4$ by adding a new vertex adjacent to one vertex in the $K_4$. I claim that $R(7K_2)=20>18=R(K_4^{+1})$. We already have $18=R(K_4)\leq R(K_4^{+1})$ and to see that $R(K_4^{+1})\leq 18$, the argument is essentially the same as proving that $R(K_4)\leq 18$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that there exists a vertex $x$ and a set $A$ with $|A|=9$ such that every edge from $x$ to $A$ is red. If there is a red triangle in $A$, we are done, so suppose not. If there is a vertex $u\in A$ with 6 blue neighbors in $A$, we are also done (since we will get a blue triangle in the blue neighborhood of $u$). Since it isn't possible for every vertex in $A$ to have blue degree $5$ to $A$, we have a vertex $v\in A$ with red degree at least 4 in $A$ and we can again see that it must be exactly 4 (otherwise we would get a blue $K_5$). Let $B$ be the set of 4 blue neighbors of $v$ in $A$. Every edge in $B$ is blue, and thus every edge from $B$ to $A\setminus B$ is red. So finally, we must have that every edge in $A\setminus B$ is blue in which case we have a blue $K_5$ and we are done. 
So the conjecture certainly needs to be updated to add the condition that it holds provided the number of edges is large enough. How large is large enough? Can anyone find a counterexample with 8 edges? We have $R(8K_2)=23$ and I wouldn't be surprised if $R(K_4^{+2})\le 22$. However, I am out of time at the moment to attempt to prove this by hand as I did above for $K_4^{+1}$. Conceivably, this could be checked computationally?
*In general, Cockyane and Lorimer "The Ramsey number for stripes" (1975) proved that for all positive integers $m$ and $r$, the $r$-color Ramsey number of $mK_2$ is $(r+1)m+(r-1)$. For $r=2$, this says $R(mK_2)=3m-1$ and in this case, the upper bound can be seen by a simple inductive argument (either we have a red edge incident to a blue edge and we can remove those three vertices and apply induction, or else every edge has the same color). The lower bound comes from taking disjoint sets $A$ and $B$ with $m-1$ and $2m-1$ vertices respectively, coloring all edges incident with $A$ red and all other edges blue.

 I just checked the Radziszowski "Small Ramsey Numbers" survey and found that surprisingly, $R(K_5-e)=22$.
So this means there is a counterexample on both 8 and 9 edges. We have $R(9K_2)=26>22=R(K_5-e)=R(K_4^{+3})$ and $R(8K_2)=23>22=R(K_5-e)\ge R(K_4^{+2})$. Since $R(10K_2)=29<43\leq R(K_5)$, perhaps it is possible that the conjecture holds provided the number of edges is at least 10?
I still don't know the exact value of $R(K_4^{+2})$ and it seems too specialized to appear in the Radziszowski survey. So this would still be interesting to know.
